description:
We bring 15+ years of software engineering and architecture experience, with expertise in AI, autonomous agents, advanced information retrieval, and delivering solutions from concept to production.

Our strengths combine hands-on development with technical leadership: designing scalable systems, building AI workflows, connecting complex data, and creating reliable, usable applications. Our experience spans aerospace, healthcare, banking, and other demanding industries.
summary:
SPHEREx Space turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky survey into films anyone can watch. 

In 1930 Pluto was found by flipping between two photographs and seeing one dot move; SPHEREx photographs the whole sky every six months in 102 colours, but its raw frames cannot be blinked: one small patch has hundreds of exposures, each in another colour, roll and pixel grid. 

SPHEREx Space indexes all 1,628,230 public SPHEREx files and keeps the index current every day. Pick any place on a globe of the sky, by dragging, by name or by coordinates, and the lab reads that patch's exposures, cleans and stacks each pass, splits it by spectrum and merges it back into one film: the background stands still, and a nearby star or a brown dwarf visibly moves. 

It detects motion itself (Barnard's Star 10.7 ± 0.8″/yr, ESA Gaia 10.4), finds asteroids inside a pass (checked with NASA JPL), and gives every object a passport with its spectrum measured live in every exposure. Find Planet X adds up exposures along trial orbits: without being told where to look it recovers Eris at 95.6 au (JPL 95.5) and Makemake, with Sedna as a strong lead. No Planet X is claimed. Free, no account, open source.
details:
Live tool: https://www.spherex.space.

Source code (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/Good-karma-lab/Planet-X-SPHEREx.

Presentation site with the 7 slides, the PDF and the 30-second film: https://good-karma-lab.github.io/Planet-X-SPHEREx/.


The problem. SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colours from 0.75 to 5 µm and returns to every place about every six months. Each exposure sees a star at another wavelength, roll angle and pixel grid, so stepping through raw frames shows the flicker of the spectrum, not the shift of a star.

How we address the challenge, point by point.

• Display SPHEREx images and make change over time easy to see. For every pass of a field all exposures are cleaned and stacked on a grid finer than the 6.15″ detector pixel, white-balanced and coloured by wavelength, then played 1 → 2 → 3 → 2 (the pendulum). Barnard's Star swings; the stars around it stand still. A Months | Days switch plays the passes or the visits of one pass.

• Help users find moving objects. Searches between passes (years), inside a pass (days) and for bodies beyond Neptune, each with a chance control and a check against catalogues.

• Enter RA and Dec. The address holds the whole state of a view, so any view is a link; the five test targets of the challenge are one click away.

• Choose the field of view. Fields of 2′ to 60′; speed rings say which motions each size keeps.

• Subtract images from different times. Difference shows each pass against the first as per-pixel significance; Co-add adds the passes.

• The 102 bands and spectra on the fly. Named bands (starlight, water vapour, methane, water ice, dust, CO₂, CO) as a blend or side by side, a wall of the six detectors, and a spectrum on a click: PSF photometry in every exposure that covers the source, drawn one point per exposure as it is measured, checked against 2MASS and WISE.

• Overlays and metadata. The Gaia check on every track, archive images (DSS2, 2MASS, AllWISE) before the SPHEREx passes, the SPHEREx pipeline flags as an artifact mask, SIMBAD and Gaia names for every clicked source.

• Easy to update with new releases. The exposure index follows NASA's public bucket (DR1 and QR3 today).
What else the tool does. A globe of the sky with the coverage of SPHEREx and the survey backgrounds; brown dwarf candidates (moving and red between 3.8 and 5 µm); the spectral anomaly map with a passport for every anomaly; ZTF and NEOWISE light curves of a clicked source; the NEOSSat frame of the comet 3I/ATLAS next to SPHEREx's film of it; the Planet X page with the predicted Planet Nine orbit, the fields searched and every search's own measured noise bar.
How it was checked (live numbers).

• Movers against Gaia: Barnard's Star 11.37 ± 0.47 ″/yr in a 5′ field and 10.7 ± 0.8 ″/yr in a 20′ field, Gaia DR3 10.4; ε Indi B 4.6 ± 0.5 ″/yr, Gaia 4.7; WISE 0855−0714, found in the red bands, 7.93 ± 0.61 ″/yr, SIMBAD 8.15 (live /api/v1/movers and /api/v1/browndwarfs, 2026-11-14).

• Asteroids found blind: on the 60′ ecliptic field of December 2025 the film search recovers 6 of the 8 known bodies brighter than V 19.1 that have at least four frames in the film, with no unmatched track in that field (live film 48c5bbb2c5e028b847075c51, JPL Small-Body Identification and Horizons, 2026-11-14).

• Chance: the same searches with the moving sources at random places make 0.0 tracks per field (20 trials on five 5′ fields and on ε Indi at 10′, 20′ and 60′); in the film search 0.0 at four or more visits and 1.83 per trial at three (12 trials), which is why a track needs four visits.

• Bodies beyond Neptune: Eris, three passes linked by one orbit, 95.6 ± 0.4 au (JPL 95.5); Makemake, two passes linked, 52.5 ± 0.2 au (JPL 52.3, not confirmed by a third pass). One pass alone gives only a wide range of distances (70 to 165 au for Eris's first pass). Live runs on www.spherex.space, 2026-11-15, keys in the Method page.

• Sedna: a blind deep sum of three passes of one field peaks at 83.0 au (JPL 83.0), 0.5 to 0.8 arcseconds from JPL's place in each pass; its 8.2σ is above the noise ceiling (8.07σ) and below the bar (8.48σ), so it is a strong lead and not a formal detection (live run, 2026-11-15).

The Method page (https://www.spherex.space/#/method) gives every step, formula and number with its source.

How it works.

A Python service reads only the image rows a field needs from NASA's public SPHEREx bucket on AWS, using an index of every Level-2 exposure with its footprint. It cleans (pipeline flags, cosmic rays by a leave-one-out test, streaks and halos; saturated cores shown white, never as holes), stacks and registers the exposures and serves versioned products; the browser draws them with WebGL. Searches and spectra run in worker processes on the server and their results are kept, so the next visitor sees them at once.

How it stays current.

Our index holds every SPHEREx Level-2 file with its footprint, 1,628,230 today (DR1 1,179,406 and QR3 448,824, equal to the bucket listing in every period). Every day at 06:00 it re-reads the last five days from IRSA and reconciles the counts with the bucket; a field's address carries a digest of its exposures, so new data re-make only the fields they touch.


Limits we state.

Find Planet X has found no new body; a peak is a lead until other data confirm it, and the depth of each search is its own measured noise bar on that field. Stars that saturate in most exposures get no SPHEREx spectrum; the motion of such a star in a small field is pulled by its saturated core. A track between passes needs three passes and a film track four visits.


Tools: Python 3.12 (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, PyArrow, SQLite), TypeScript with Preact and WebGL (Vite, three.js), pytest, ruff, mypy, vitest, Playwright, Caddy, one Oracle Cloud VM. Built with AI coding assistants (Anthropic's Claude Code) under the team's direction; every picture is computed from real NASA SPHEREx exposures, none is AI-generated. In the 30-second demo video, two clips are AI-generated (Google Gemini, marked on screen) and the voice-over and sound effects are AI-made (ElevenLabs).
dataRefs: SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images, DR1 and QR3 (NASA/IPAC IRSA)
IRSA HiPS sky surveys: DSS2, 2MASS, WISE
WISE, AllWISE and NEOWISE catalogues and light curves (IRSA)
JPL Horizons (ephemerides of known bodies and of the spacecraft)
JPL Small-Body Identification API (known asteroids in a film)
NASA SVS Deep Star Maps 2020 (the star map of the globe)
projectRefs: ESA Gaia DR3 (the check of every moving track, names, distances)
CSA NEOSSat (frame of comet 3I/ATLAS), Canadian Astronomy Data Centre
SIMBAD, CDS Strasbourg (object names and types)
SVO Filter Profile Service (filter curves for the photometry check)
Minor Planet Center (observatory codes, ADES format)
SPHEREx Space source code (Apache-2.0), with the full list of data and references
SPHEREx Space presentation site (7 slides, PDF, 30-second film)
